title: list, span, and buffer
blurb:
Name a better duo than `ptr` and `len`, I'll wait. `list` in `k1` is the growable one (a dynamic array), backed by a `buffer`.

`buffer[t]` is the raw construct that means 'this is memory that holds `t`s'. `span[t]` is your read-only, typically borrowed view of a buffer often called a slice, but I don't like how that implies cutting or partiality. Those closures disappear at runtime, by the way

title: Structs
blurb: Structs let us say 'and' at the type level. They're the basic building block of all data composition. `k1` has both named and anonymous structs, and understands their structure and lets you talk about it like typescript. More on that later

blocks.label: program

title: either
blurb: `either`s let us say 'or' at the typelevel. Together with structs, we can 'and' and 'or' our way to extremely powerful constructs. This combination is often called "Algebraic Data Types". `k1` will construct a bare integer enum at runtime, or a tagged union, depending on whether any of your variants have payloads. Core types like `result` and `opt` will be familiar to Rust users, and are defined as simply as this. `?u8` is shorthand for `opt[u8]` and is a 2 byte struct at runtime

blocks.label: in core
blocks.code:
type opt[t] = either { none, some(t) }
type result[t, e] = either { ok(t), err(e) }

title: First-class functions and lambdas
blurb: Lambdas compile to bare metal functions. `some fn int -> int`, shorthand for `some fn(int) -> int`, selects the physical representation for that function and specializes on it: a direct call for a named function or a lambda, an indirect call through a `*fn`, a dynamic call through a `dyn[fn]`.

blocks.label: program

title: Abilities
blurb: k1 uses `ability` to model define and implement interfaces, and do all kinds of ad-hoc polymorphism, that leaves no runtime trace. `impl ours/greet for theirs/cat` is an independent 3rd party, neither the cat nor greet, teaching cat how to greet. This is an immensely powerful decoupling, contrast with inheritance-based implementation. An ability can have both ability-side and impl-side type parameters. `to[t]` is an ability-side parameter; a type can be `to` for as many `t`s as it can convert to; but `iterable[t]` is an impl-side parameter: a type can implement iterator _once_ and provide only one type that it iterates over. (similar to Rust traits' associated types)

title: Generics
blurb: Types and functions can accept types as parameters; this is your standard parametric polymorphism ('inputs over shapes') that allows writing code we call 'generic'. This happens entirely at compile-time, and understands abilities as type-bounds.

title: References
blurb: These are really just pointers. They are nonnull, but it's not that hard to manufacture a null one; I'm not too interested in stopping you. The untyped one, your `void*`, is called `ptr`.
